sentences.text: The holotype specimen CEUM 5071 is a partial skeleton lacking a skull that belonged to a juvenile individual, while two other fragmentary skeletons represent subadults. All three known specimens were disarticulated and heavily eroded because they were exposed at the surface before discovery.

The paratype specimens, though not yet fully grown, were about 3 meters long. Nedcolbertia possessed a thumb claw that was much larger than its second hand claw. The femur had a lesser trochanter clearly lower than the greater trochanter and a well-developed fourth trochanter. It lacked an arctometatarsal foot structure and did not have an enlarged second foot claw.
The vertebrae of Nedcolbertia were not heavily pneumatized.
The specific name justinhofmanni honors Justin Hofmann, a six-year-old boy from Newton, New Jersey, who won a contest sponsored by Discover Card.
Its thumb claw was much larger than its second hand claw, a feature distinct from many other small theropods.

Three theropod skeletons were discovered in 1993 by Christopher Whittle near Cisco in the basal Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah. Although announced in 1996 as "Nedcolbertia whittlei", the species was formally described and named Nedcolbertia justinhofmanni in 1998 by Kirkland, Whittle, Britt, Madsen, and Burge. The genus name Nedcolbertia honors the American paleontologist Edwin Harris Colbert, who was known as "Ned" to his friends.
Nedcolbertia is very similar to its close relatives Ornitholestes and Compsognathus. Kirkland described Nedcolbertia as a "small coelurosaurian related to Ornitholestes" in his report.
The original describers assigned Nedcolbertia with certainty to Tetanurae and provisionally to Coelurosauria. Nedcolbertia is classified within the unranked family Coelurosauria.

A 2016 study suggested Nedcolbertia is an ornithomimosaur based on comparisons with remains from the Arundel Formation, Harpymimus, and Nqwebasaurus. In 2024, Cau suggested Nedcolbertia possibly belongs to Allosauroidea but placed it within Megalosauroidea in his analysis.

Nedcolbertia was a theropod dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous Valanginian age in the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah. Nedcolbertia lived at the beginning of the Cretaceous period, approximately 130 million years ago, in what is now North America. The fossil record for Nedcolbertia spans from 137.05 to 132.6 million years ago.
